title: Nobody wins, one colour takes over
hook: Neither beetle colour is better. Does the half-and-half mix stay put?

doesNotKnow: that variant frequencies wander by chance alone
that a variant can be lost or take over with no advantage
that population size sets how fast this happens

misconception: If neither variant is better, the mix stays at about 50:50.
objective: The learner can explain that in a finite population each generation is a random sample of the last, so variant shares wander until one is lost and the other takes over, and that this happens much faster in small populations.

claims.text: When each new generation is a random draw of parents from the last, variant shares change by chance alone (genetic drift), even when neither variant is better.
claims.source: Wright-Fisher model; Gillespie, J. H. (2004), Population Genetics: A Concise Guide, 2nd ed., Johns Hopkins University Press, ch. 2; Hartl & Clark, Principles of Population Genetics, ch. on random genetic drift.

claims.text: Once a colour is lost it never comes back (without mutation or beetles arriving from elsewhere), so populations end up all one colour.
claims.source: With share 0 or 1, every draw copies the same colour: both are absorbing states. The model in Demo.tsx has no mutation and no migration.

claims.text: With 20 beetles, most populations are all one colour within a few dozen generations; with 200, after 100 generations most are still mixed.
claims.source: 4,000 seeded runs of the stage model (haploid Wright-Fisher, start 50%): N = 20 fixed by generation 30 in 71%, by 60 in 94%, by 100 in 99%; N = 200 fixed by generation 100 in 14%. Stage seed 1: all five N = 20 lanes fixed by generation 41; one of five N = 200 lanes fixed at generation 100.

claims.text: For a variant with no advantage, the chance it eventually takes over equals its starting share, here 1 in 2.
claims.source: Kimura, M. (1962), 'On the probability of fixation of mutant genes in a population', Genetics 47: 713-719 (neutral case u(p) = p). Simulation check: red took over in 50.5% (N = 20) and 52.0% (N = 200) of 4,000 runs.

claims.text: The model has no mutation, no selection and no migration; beetles and colours are made up.
claims.source: Modelling choice stated in the reveal.

recall.question: Two islands start with the same 50:50 mix of two harmless flower colours. One has 30 plants, the other 30,000. After 200 generations, which is more likely to have lost a colour?
options: Equally likely: neither colour is better
recall.why: Each generation is a random sample of the last. Small samples swing more, so the small island drifts to one colour far sooner.
